body.statement: The exact law \(\omega^\star\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\), has \(K^0=K^1=\begin{psmallmatrix}29/5&-12/5\\8/5&1/5\end{psmallmatrix}\) with ordered spectrum \((5,1)\), and satisfies \(\tau_1=(1/25,0,-1/25)\), \(\tau_2=(-1/40,-1/40,1/20)\), and \(\tau=(3/400,-1/80,1/200)\). By contrast, \(P^A\) and \(P^B\) induce the same observed five-date law, active slices, and cycle product while their type shares are \((3/5,2/5)\) and \((2/5,3/5)\), respectively, and their type-specific exit ATT pairs are \((-2/75,1/20)\) and \((-1/25,1/30)\). Hence deleting \(\text{ass:no-date-one-absorption}\) destroys identification of type masses and conditional type effects, although this pair leaves the aggregate exit ATT equal to \(1/250\).
body.justification: The witness establishes nonvacuity, checks every normalization exactly, and identifies the precise role of the initial support face for the conditional targets.
body.gap: Existing absorbing-outcome DiD results do not provide a two-type multi-state observational-equivalence calculation, and generic mixture results do not isolate the initial-absorber allocation that breaks conditional ATT recovery.
body.consumer: Applied researchers can treat baseline exit as a falsifiable support diagnostic and avoid interpreting conditional latent-type effects when baseline absorbers are present.
body.proof_tex:
We first verify that the construction in \texttt{def:exact-witness} defines a law with every property required by \texttt{def:face-model}.  A convenient explicit coupling of the two potential paths is the following.  Put \(R_{j,0}=Q_j\) and \(R_{j,1}=V_j\).  For \(d\in\{0,1\}\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), \(s_0\in\mathcal A\), and all remaining states in \(\mathcal S\), define the joint mass of
\[
 (D,Z,S_0,S_1,S_2,X_3(0),X_4(0),X_3(1),X_4(1))
 =(d,j,s_0,s_1,s_2,u_0,w_0,u_1,w_1)
\]
to be
\[
 \frac18 H_j[s_0,s_1]Q_j[s_1,s_2]
 Q_j[s_2,u_0]Q_j[u_0,w_0]
 V_j[s_2,u_1]V_j[u_1,w_1],                                      \tag{1}
\]
and give mass zero when \(s_0\notin\mathcal A\).  Every displayed matrix has nonnegative entries and satisfies
\[
 H_j\mathbf 1_3=Q_j\mathbf 1_3=V_j\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_3,
 \qquad
 H_j[e,{:}]=Q_j[e,{:}]=V_j[e,{:}]=(0,0,1).                       \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, summing (1) successively over \(w_0,u_0,w_1,u_1,s_2,s_1,s_0,j,d\) gives one, so (1) is a probability law.  Set \(X_t(r)=S_t\) for \(t\leq2\) and \(r\in\{0,1\}\), and set the observed state to \(X_t=X_t(D)\).  This proves consistency and no anticipation.  Marginalizing the continuation belonging to the other treatment path in (1) leaves a first-order Markov factorization conditional on \((D,Z)\): its transitions are \(H_j,Q_j,Q_j,Q_j\) for \(r=0\) and \(H_j,Q_j,V_j,V_j\) for \(r=1\).  Thus \texttt{ass:markov-paths} holds.  Equation (2), together with inspection of the active rows in \texttt{def:exact-witness}, proves support on \(\mathcal G\) and \texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}.  Moreover,
\[
 P(D=d)=\frac12,\qquad P(Z=j\mid D=d)=\frac12,                 \tag{3}
\]
so cohort and type overlap hold and both type support points occur.  Taking \(H_j^d=H_j\), \(U_j=Q_j\), and \(L_j=Q_j\) verifies all three declared common untreated-transition restrictions.  Finally, \(S_0\in\mathcal A\) almost surely and \(H_j[x,e]=0\) for \(x\in\mathcal A\), whence
\[
 P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=0                                             \tag{4}
\]
for both cohorts.  This verifies \texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption}.

It remains to check the two rank conditions and the numerical conclusions.  For \(x\in\mathcal A\), introduce the component predecessor matrix
\[
 B_x[u,j]=P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d)
          =\frac14H_j[u,x].                                     \tag{5}
\]
It does not depend on \(d\), and direct substitution gives
\[
 B_a=\begin{pmatrix}3/16&1/12\\1/16&1/6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_b=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&1/6\\3/16&1/12\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det(B_a)=\frac5{192},\quad \det(B_b)=-\frac5{192}.           \tag{6}
\]
Let \(D_{xy}=\operatorname{diag}(Q_1[x,y],Q_2[x,y])\), and let row \(j\) of \(C_y^0\) be row \(y\) of \(Q_j\), while row \(j\) of \(C_y^1\) is row \(y\) of \(V_j\).  Conditional first-order Markov factorization and summation over \(Z\) yield, entry by entry,
\[
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 =\sum_{j=1}^2B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y^d[j,v],
 \qquad A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}C_y^d.                                \tag{7}
\]
For the active terminal minors, direct calculation gives
\[
 \det(\bar C_a^0)=\frac9{50},\quad
 \det(\bar C_b^0)=-\frac3{100},\quad
 \det(\bar C_a^1)=\frac{31}{100},\quad
 \det(\bar C_b^1)=-\frac1{20}.                                 \tag{8}
\]
Using \(\det(\bar A_{xy}^d)=\det(B_x)Q_1[x,y]Q_2[x,y]\det(\bar C_y^d)\), equations (6)--(8) give, in the order \((aa,ab,ba,bb)\),
\[
 \bigl(\det\bar A_{aa}^0,\det\bar A_{ab}^0,
       \det\bar A_{ba}^0,\det\bar A_{bb}^0\bigr)
 =\left(\frac9{16000},-\frac3{32000},-\frac9{32000},\frac3{12800}\right), \tag{9}
\]
and
\[
 \bigl(\det\bar A_{aa}^1,\det\bar A_{ab}^1,
       \det\bar A_{ba}^1,\det\bar A_{bb}^1\bigr)
 =\left(\frac{31}{32000},-\frac1{6400},-\frac{31}{64000},\frac1{2560}\right). \tag{10}
\]
Every number in (9)--(10) is nonzero.  Hence every one of the eight active slices is nonsingular; since there are finitely many of them, the minimum of their positive smallest singular values is positive.  This is exactly \texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}.

Restricting (7) to active terminal columns and multiplying the four factors in the order specified by \texttt{def:observed-slices} cancels \(\bar C_a^d,B_b,\bar C_b^d\) and gives
\[
 K^d
 =B_aD_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}B_a^{-1}.              \tag{11}
\]
All divisions in (11) are legitimate because the relevant active entries of \(Q_1,Q_2\) are strictly positive.  The middle diagonal matrix is
\[
 D_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}
 =\operatorname{diag}\!\left(
 \frac{(3/5)(1/2)}{(1/5)(3/10)},
 \frac{(1/5)(3/5)}{(3/10)(2/5)}\right)
 =\operatorname{diag}(5,1).                                    \tag{12}
\]
Writing \(B_a=48^{-1}\begin{psmallmatrix}9&4\\3&8\end{psmallmatrix}\), equations (11)--(12) therefore imply, for both \(d=0\) and \(d=1\),
\[
 K^d
 =\frac1{60}
 \begin{pmatrix}45&4\\15&8\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}8&-4\\-3&9\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}29/5&-12/5\\8/5&1/5\end{pmatrix}.             \tag{13}
\]
Its trace and determinant are \(6\) and \(5\), respectively, so
\[
 \det(\lambda I_2-K^d)=\lambda^2-6\lambda+5=(\lambda-5)(\lambda-1),
 \qquad g^d=\sqrt{6^2-4\cdot5}=4>0.                            \tag{14}
\]
Thus the ordered spectrum is \((5,1)\), and \texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum} holds.  Equations (2)--(4), (9)--(10), and (14), together with the preceding structural checks, verify every member property in \texttt{def:face-model}; hence \(\omega^\star\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).

We next compute the causal effects rather than defining them from the observed recovery formula.  The uniform initial law is invariant under each \(H_j\), and therefore the type-specific date-two laws in the treated cohort are
\[
 p_{2,1}^1=(1/2,1/2,0)H_1Q_1=(2/5,2/5,1/5),
 \qquad
 p_{2,2}^1=(1/2,1/2,0)H_2Q_2=(1/4,1/2,1/4).                    \tag{15}
\]
By no anticipation in the coupling (1), both potential paths have the same \(X_2\); conditioning on \((X_2,Z,D=1)\) and using the transition factors in (1) thus yields the causal identity
\[
 \tau_j=p_{2,j}^1(V_j-Q_j).                                    \tag{16}
\]
The two multiplications in (16) are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau_1
 &= (2/5,2/5,1/5)
 \begin{pmatrix}1/10&-1/10&0\\0&1/10&-1/10\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
   =(1/25,0,-1/25),\\
 \tau_2
 &= (1/4,1/2,1/4)
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1/10&-1/10\\-1/20&-1/10&3/20\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
   =(-1/40,-1/40,1/20).
 \end{aligned}                                                  \tag{17}
\]
This derives the potential-outcome contrasts in the proposition directly from the constructed law.  By (3) and the definition of the aggregate ATT,
\[
 \tau=\frac12\tau_1+\frac12\tau_2
      =(3/400,-1/80,1/200).                                    \tag{18}
\]

Finally consider \texttt{def:outside-face-pair}.  Let the added component have \(X_t(0)=X_t(1)=e\) for every \(t\).  Conditional on either cohort, both \(P^A\) and \(P^B\) put mass \(4/5\) on the law \(\omega^\star\) and mass \(1/5\) on this all-exit path; they differ only in whether the latent label of the added component is \(1\) or \(2\).  Thus for every state path \(x_{0:4}\),
\[
 P^A(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
 =P^B(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
 =\frac45P_{\omega^\star}(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
  +\frac15\mathbf 1\{x_{0:4}=(e,e,e,e,e)\}.                   \tag{19}
\]
The cohort law is also the same, so (19) proves equality of the complete observed five-date laws.  The two enlarged laws retain all assumptions in \texttt{def:face-model} except (4).  In particular, the conditional Markov property is not lost by mixing: at any active current state the all-exit component has posterior probability zero, so the next-state row is the original active row; at current state \(e\), both mixture components move to \(e\) with probability one by \texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}.  Hence the transition depends only on the current state, \((D,Z)\), and the relevant date, and every common untreated kernel remains \(Q_j\) on active rows with absorbing row \((0,0,1)\).  On the other hand,
\[
 P^A(X_1=e\mid D=d)=P^B(X_1=e\mid D=d)=\frac15,                \tag{20}
\]
so these laws lie outside precisely the declared no-date-one-absorption face.

Because the all-exit path contributes to none of the slices indexed by \(x,y\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 A_{xy}^{A,d}=A_{xy}^{B,d}=\frac45A_{xy}^{\omega^\star,d},
 \qquad
 \bar A_{xy}^{A,d}=\bar A_{xy}^{B,d}=\frac45\bar A_{xy}^{\omega^\star,d}. \tag{21}
\]
Thus all active slices remain nonsingular.  The four scalar factors in the cycle product cancel as
\[
 \left(\frac45\right)
 \left(\frac45\right)^{-1}
 \left(\frac45\right)
 \left(\frac45\right)^{-1}=1,                                 \tag{22}
\]
so both laws retain the matrix (13) and its ordered type signatures \(5>1\).  The active part has conditional mass \((4/5)(1/2)=2/5\) for each type.  Allocation of the added \(1/5\) therefore gives
\[
 (\pi_1^{A,d},\pi_2^{A,d})=(3/5,2/5),
 \qquad
 (\pi_1^{B,d},\pi_2^{B,d})=(2/5,3/5).                          \tag{23}
\]
The all-exit component has state-effect vector \(\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_e=0\).  Hence, for \(C\in\{A,B\}\), the conditional-effect numerators obey
\[
 \pi_j^{C,1}\tau_j^C
 =E_C\!\left[\mathbf 1\{Z=j\}
   \{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\}
   \mid D=1\right]
 =\frac25\tau_j^{\omega^\star}.                               \tag{24}
\]
Dividing (24) by the strictly positive masses in (23), and then taking the exit coordinate of (17), gives
\[
 (\tau_{1,e}^A,\tau_{2,e}^A)=(-2/75,1/20),
 \qquad
 (\tau_{1,e}^B,\tau_{2,e}^B)=(-1/25,1/30).                     \tag{25}
\]
Their common aggregate exit effect is nevertheless
\[
 \tau_e^C=\sum_{j=1}^2\pi_j^{C,1}\tau_{j,e}^C
 =\frac25\left(-\frac1{25}+\frac1{20}\right)=\frac1{250},
 \qquad C\in\{A,B\}.                                         \tag{26}
\]
Equations (19), (23), and (25) exhibit two laws in the model obtained by deleting \texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption} that have the same observed law but different type masses and different conditional type effects.  Therefore no functional of that observed law can equal either of those conditional latent-type targets throughout the enlarged compatible fiber.  Equation (26) records, without overclaiming, that this particular pair does not separate the aggregate exit ATT.
